Cons:
Very small — gear ratio means higher rotation distance config needed
More expensive than printed Sherpa Micro alternatives
Limited reseller availability
Not ideal for high-torque abrasive filament applications
Description: The SLM Sherpa Micro is Lettucehead3D's SLM metal-printed version of the Sherpa Micro RC2, using the 6T motor variant. SLM printing produces near-solid metal density without the porosity of cast or sintered parts. The 6T motor runs cooler than the 8T, reducing heat transfer into the filament path.
Verdict Label: SLM-printed near-solid-metal density in the smallest Sherpa format — cooler-running 6T motor is the real differentiator.
Name: SLM Sherpa Micro
Pros:
SLM (Selective Laser Melting) metal printing — near-tool-steel density
Based on Sherpa Micro RC2 — latest revision with 6T motor
6T motor runs cooler than 8T — less heat transferred to filament
Smallest and lightest extruder in the SLM lineup
Direct from Lettucehead3D — quality-controlled production

Cons: Same $312 price as standard Pro Metal but HT motor is the only meaningful differentiator; extremely niche — only needed in true heated enclosure builds; heavy and large
Description: Thermal-hardened variant of the LGX Pro Metal, designed for heated chamber 3D printers. The key differentiator from the standard LGX Pro Metal 1.75 is the High Temperature Nema17 30mm HT pancake motor that maintains reliable performance at elevated ambient temperatures. Aluminum housing throughout (vs PA12 GF polymer on LGX PRO). Full hardened steel drive train. Same $312.38 price as the standard Pro Metal. Luke's Lab specifically recommends this extruder paired with the Chube conduction hotend for heated chamber builds. Not needed for standard enclosed printers.
Verdict Label: Niche Pick
Name: Bondtech LGX Pro Metal HT
Pros: Aluminum housing (fully metal body); HT high-temperature Nema17 30mm motor designed for heated chamber operation; full hardened steel drive train; maximum thermal resistance of any LGX extruder; recommended by Luke's Lab for Chube hotend pairings

Cons: $70-96 USD is expensive vs. a printed Sherpa Mini; motor sold separately; same 50:17 gear ratio as older designs
Description: The official Annex Engineering CNC Sherpa Mini v3 design, manufactured by Fysetc. Ditches the printed body for CNC machined aluminum throughout, adds a PEEK filament path and PEEK GF30 reinforced spur gear. Drop-in replacement for any Sherpa Mini toolhead with significant durability and precision gains. Note: different product from the Fysetc Sherpa V3 (Fysetc's own printed-body design).
Verdict Label: Best-in-class Sherpa Mini — CNC precision with PEEK filament path
Name: CNC Sherpa Mini v3 (Annex/Fysetc)
Pros: Fully CNC machined aluminum body; PEEK GF30 50t spur gear; nano-coated drive gears; PEEK filament path; metal ECAS inlet; 45g without motor; drop-in for any Sherpa Mini toolhead

Cons: Bowden only — not suitable for direct drive toolheads; introduces filament lag compared to direct drive; larger and heavier than DD extruders; less common in modern Voron builds
Description: VoronDesign's official remote extruder, designed for Bowden or multi-material setups where the extruder mounts to the frame rather than the toolhead. Strong gear reduction handles long filament paths reliably. The standard choice when building a Voron with a remote drive or multi-material system.
Verdict Label: Bowden/Remote Drive — Official Voron for frame-mounted or multi-material setups
Name: Voron M4 (Möbius 4)
Pros: Official VoronDesign extruder; purpose-built for remote/Bowden drive; strong grip for long filament paths; free/OSS; well-documented; standard for MMU/multi-material Voron configurations

Cons: $312 USD is very expensive; large and heavy form factor; limited Voron-specific toolhead mount support; overkill for unenclosed or standard-temp builds
Description: Bondtech's all-metal extruder with full steel drive gears and CNC metal housing, designed for sustained high-temperature chamber printing where plastic bodies would soften or deform. Highlighted by Luke's Lab as a strong pairing with the Chube conduction hotend in heated chamber enclosures. Available in 1.75mm and 2.85mm variants.
Verdict Label: All-Metal Premium — Heated chamber builds, CHT/Chube hotend pairing
Name: Bondtech LGX Pro Metal
Pros: Full steel drive train; all-metal body engineered for sustained high-temp chamber use; large LGX gear ratio; no plastic parts to soften at elevated temps; 2.85mm variant available; highlighted by Luke's Lab for Chube conduction hotend pairing

Cons:
Ecosystem-specific — designed for VzBot/HevORT custom mounts
Single-drive twirl gear — less filament grip than dual BMG-style
Limited toolhead support outside VzBot ecosystem
Fewer guides and less documentation than Voron-standard extruders
Description: CNC-machined 6061 aluminum extruder originally designed by MirageC as the HextrudORT, adapted for VzBot by the VzBoT3D community. Uses a single-drive twirl gear: 60T main gear with 8T pinion (7.5:1) or 10T pinion (6:1). Available in Standard, PLUS (larger 60T gear), and Low/WC (low center of gravity) variants. Commercial versions manufactured by Mellow3D and distributed through West3D and Fabreeko. Drive type: Single. Mount: VzBot custom — not Voron-standard. Ecosystem: VzBot 330, VZ235, HevORT.
Verdict Label: The definitive VzBot/HevORT extruder — excellent CNC quality, but ecosystem-locked.
Name: Vz-HextrudORT
Pros:
CNC 6061 aluminum body — extremely rigid and light
Low center of gravity variant improves dynamic print quality
Open-source with active VzBoT community iteration
Multiple variants (Standard, PLUS, Low/WC) for different build requirements
Mellow3D commercial version available through major US/EU resellers

Cons: Community mod with less formal documentation, specific to modified AntHead setups
Description: Community-modified variant of the G2 WristWatch AntHead, with additional tweaks to geometry or mounting for improved fitment or compatibility in specific small-format printer builds. Open-source, print-it-yourself.
Name: G2 WW AntHead Modified
Pros: Community-refined fit, retains full 9:1 G2 torque

Cons: Large form factor not suited to compact toolheads; $187 is steep when LGX Lite PRO exists for $149; limited community adoption vs Lite platform
Description: Industrial-targeted evolution of the base LGX. Upgrades the motor from 25mm to a stronger 30mm Nema17 pancake and includes the full hardened steel drive train stock (no separate purchase needed). PA12 GF glass-filled polymer housing provides higher thermal resistance than standard LGX. A free aluminum interface plug accommodates longer hotends. Tagged by Bondtech as industrial/PROduction-grade. Sits between the base LGX ($123) and Pro Metal ($312) in price and specification.
Verdict Label: Solid Choice
Name: Bondtech LGX PRO
Pros: Stronger 30mm Nema17 motor vs base LGX; full hardened steel drive train included from factory; PA12 GF housing for higher thermal resistance; free aluminum interface plug supports longer hotends

Cons: 75g without motor is heavy by modern standards; $100 is expensive for what you get; superseded on weight and price by community designs that use its own gear set
Description: The BMG popularized dual-drive on desktop 3D printers. Its 50:17 gear ratio and precision hardened steel drive gears set the standard every subsequent extruder is compared against. Still sold and supported, but at $100 and 75g it has been outclassed by lighter designs like the Sherpa Mini and Orbiter using the same gearing.
Verdict Label: Legacy Classic — Reliable but heavy vs. modern alternatives
Name: Bondtech BMG
Pros: Proven dual-drive technology; 50:17 gear ratio baseline used by dozens of community designs; bowden or direct drive; wide mount compatibility; abundant community support and documentation

Cons: Requires compatible LDO motor, plastic gearbox housing can be fragile under heavy load, no hands-on community data yet on long-term durability vs v2.0
Description: Refined successor to the Orbiter v2.0. Key improvements: knurled spider shaft reduces eccentricity to 20-30µm (vs. 50-140µm on v2.0); wide-cut flat-bottom RNC-coated gears at HRC60+; new MF679ZZ bearing (9mm inner bore vs. MF148ZZ on v2.0). Same 7.5:1 gear ratio and identical Klipper settings to v2.0 — firmware-transparent upgrade. Available as an upgrade kit for genuine LDO Orbiter v2.0 units.
Name: Orbiter v2.5
Pros: Exceptionally precise drive gear contact, very lightweight at 18g, upgrade path from v2.0, widely supported across toolheads, planetary gearbox reliability

Cons: Requires specific pinion stepper motor, plastic body less rigid than CNC alternatives, older design showing age vs newer competitors
Description: Dual-geared hobbed filament extruder designed by Anlin / Annex Engineering. Gear-driven design for high torque with near-silent operation. Release 2 adds Bondtech RIDGA v2 compatibility and a stronger idler arm. Requires a pinion-equipped pancake stepper (Nema 14). Print-it-yourself open-source design with commercial gear kits available.
Verdict Label: The print-it-yourself lightweight dual-drive standard — massive toolhead support, near-silent operation, and free to build.
Name: Sherpa Mini
Pros: Extremely light (~25g without motor), massive toolhead ecosystem support, near-silent operation, print-it-yourself with accessible gear kits

Cons: Smaller body means reduced gear contact patch, limited to micro-format toolheads, less toolhead ecosystem support than Sherpa Mini
Description: Smaller sibling of the Sherpa Mini, designed for ultra-compact toolheads and Printers for Ants (V0-scale). Maintains the same 50:17 dual-gear drive ratio in a significantly reduced footprint. Open-source, print-it-yourself.
Name: Sherpa Micro
Pros: Extremely compact and lightweight (~18g without motor), purpose-built for V0-scale builds, proven Annex Engineering design heritage

Cons: Still a printed-plastic body, less established than Sherpa or Orbiter in the community
Description: Updated version of the ProtoXtruder with refined geometry, improved idler arm, and better component compatibility. Print-it-yourself open-source design on Printables. Community-driven improvements over v1 with wider hardware compatibility.
Name: ProtoXtruder 2.0
Pros: Free to print, improved over v1 with better idler and geometry, active community support

Cons: Requires specific toolhead compatibility, smaller motor means slightly reduced max current
Description: Compact variant of the Galileo 2 gearbox redesigned for small-format printers and V0-scale toolheads. Maintains the 9:1 planetary gear ratio in a significantly smaller footprint. Community name 'WristWatch' refers to its compact round profile. Print-it-yourself open-source design.
Name: G2 WristWatch (G2 WW)
Pros: Full 9:1 G2 torque in a compact package, ideal for V0 and small toolheads, open-source

Cons: Specific to AntHead toolhead, limited standalone use
Description: WristWatch G2 variant specifically adapted for the AntHead toolhead. Uses the same 9:1 G2 planetary gearbox in the WristWatch compact format, mounted to the AntHead body. Open-source, print-it-yourself.
Name: G2 WW AntHead
Pros: Full G2 torque, purpose-designed AntHead integration, open-source

Cons:
Superseded by v2.5 for new builds (tighter gear tolerances)
Higher gear eccentricity than v2.5 (50–140µm vs 20–30µm)
Requires matched motor from LDO or equivalent — not universal stepper
Description: The Orbiter v2.0 is a lightweight dual-drive direct extruder by Claude Remy / Orbiter Projects. Uses a 7.5:1 gear reduction with hardened BMG-quality drive gears gripping filament from both sides. Klipper: rotation_distance 4.69, gear_ratio 7.5:1, 16 microsteps. LDO Motors produces an official kit including a matched pancake stepper. The v2.5 improves gear eccentricity (20–30µm vs 50–140µm) but uses identical firmware settings — both share the same BOM. Drive type: Dual. Ecosystem: Voron/CoreXY universal.
Verdict Label: The extruder that set the lightweight high-ratio standard for Voron — still excellent, v2.5 is the precision upgrade.
Name: Orbiter v2.0
Pros:
Exceptionally lightweight at 18g body
Massive toolhead compatibility across Voron ecosystem
Hardened dual-drive gears for reliable grip
LDO kit available with matched pancake motor
Direct upgrade path to v2.5
Extensive community documentation and Klipper profiles

Cons:
PEEK gears are harder to source as replacements than POM
More expensive than printed Sherpa alternatives
10T version requires rotation distance recalibration vs 8T
Description: The Fysetc Sherpa V3 is the third-generation CNC version of the Sherpa Mini extruder. The key upgrade over V2 is the replacement of POM gears with PEEK (30% glass fiber) gears and PEEK motor inserts, specifically solving the heat creep and TPU clogging issue that affected earlier all-metal Sherpa builds. CNC aviation aluminum body, Moons 36 motor, nano-coated steel drive gears.
Verdict Label: The most refined CNC Sherpa available — PEEK gears and inserts solve the TPU heat creep problem.
Name: Sherpa V3
Pros:
PEEK (30% GF) gears replace POM — dramatically better thermal isolation from motor
PEEK inserts added to further block motor heat transfer
CNC aviation aluminum body — lightweight and stiff
Nano-coated mold steel drive gears — durable and precise
Moons 36 pancake motor included
Supports both 8T and 10T configurations
Direct and Bowden compatible

Cons: Requires Galileo 2 compatible toolhead mount, slightly heavier than ultra-light options
Description: Full redesign over Galileo 1, moving to a 9:1 planetary gear ratio. Uses a custom 9T stepper with 20% higher contact surface area than 10T designs, and proper 3-planet meshing (9T sun / 3 planets) for even loading and better wear. Klipper: rotation_distance 47.088, gear_ratio 9:1, run_current 0.6A. Open-sourced by JaredC01.
Name: Galileo 2 Extruder (G2E)
Pros: High torque 9:1 ratio, excellent gear meshing, open-source design with LDO quality manufacturing, proven reliability across Voron community

Cons: Printed body; gear kit must be purchased separately; four sub-variants adds selection overhead; open design less protected than enclosed extruders
Description: An open-air printed extruder body series from chirpy2605 that reuses gear sets from other extruders. Four variants: LGX Lite, Trianglelab TBG, Orbiter v1.5, and Orbiter v2.0. The open design makes gear mesh inspection and backlash adjustment straightforward. All variants are free/OSS on GitHub.
Verdict Label: Open-Air Design — 4 gear variants, easy inspection and backlash tuning
Name: RoundTrip
Pros: Open air design lets you see and inspect gear mesh directly; four variants (LGX Lite, TBG Lite, Orbiter v1.5, Orbiter v2.0 gears); backlash adjustment on LGX and TBG variants; from chirpy2605 (Dragon Burner designer); free/OSS

Cons: Printed plastic body less precise than CNC alternatives, v1 superseded by v2.0
Description: Open-source print-it-yourself extruder from Printables designed for prosumer CoreXY builds. Uses standard Bondtech-style dual gears. Intended as a more accessible alternative to commercial extruders with a focus on simple assembly and widely available hardware.
Name: ProtoXtruder v1
Pros: Free to print, standard hardware BOM, good community support on Printables

Cons: Nema14 limits max torque vs Nema17 options; LGX Lite mount requires compatible toolhead bracket
Description: Updated LGX Lite featuring Bondtech's Steel Drive Train (2022 hardened steel gears) installed from factory, and PA12 GF glass-filled polymer housing for improved thermal resistance. Same compact Nema14 20mm pancake form factor and 44:10 gear ratio as the original LGX Lite, but ships ready to run without the $43 steel drive train upgrade purchase. At $116.25 it's $16 less than the LGX Lite PRO with a solid featureset for most builds. Strong choice for Voron, RatRig, and other LGX-Lite-compatible toolheads.
Verdict Label: Top Pick
Name: Bondtech LGX Lite V2
Pros: Steel Drive Train pre-installed from factory (vs $43 upgrade on base Lite); PA12 GF housing for better thermal tolerance; complete kit with Nema14 20mm pancake included; compact LGX Lite footprint

Cons: Steel drive train costs $43 extra (not included); 25mm motor weaker than PRO; large form factor vs compact alternatives
Description: The original Bondtech LGX (Large Gears eXtruder), introduced 2021 as Gen3 dual-drive platform. Uses physically larger drive gears than BMG for improved filament grip. Comes with a custom Nema17 25mm pancake motor and supports both bowden and direct drive. Steel Drive Train is a $43.63 optional upgrade (pre-installed on LGX Lite V2 and LGX PRO). Extensive upgrade kit ecosystem covers most popular printers. At $123.75 it's the entry point to the full-size LGX platform.
Verdict Label: Solid Choice
Name: Bondtech LGX
Pros: Gen3 large dual-drive gears for improved grip; includes Nema17 25mm pancake; bowden or direct drive; massive ecosystem of printer-specific upgrade kits

Cons: Fewer toolhead-native integrations than G2E, slightly less community documentation for standalone builds
Description: Galileo 2 extruder configured as a pure standalone unit — uses the same G2 gearbox (9:1, 9T sun/3 planets) but mounts independently without requiring a specific toolhead carriage integration. Shares BOM and printed parts with the G2E kit. Klipper config identical to G2E. Open-sourced by JaredC01.
Name: Galileo 2 Standalone (Hartk)
Pros: Flexible mounting, high 9:1 torque, interchangeable with G2E hardware, open-source

Cons:
This is a gear assembly, not a complete extruder — requires a compatible extruder body
Higher cost than standard BMG gear replacements
Limited to specific extruder body compatibility
Most builders won't need this vs standard Annex/Bondtech gear kits
Description: NOTE: The RIDGA v2 is an OEM gear assembly kit, not a complete extruder. Reversed Integrated Drive Gear Assembly v2 by Bondtech. Designed as an upgrade/replacement for standard BMG-style dual-drive gear sets used in extruders like the Sherpa Mini. Features an improved reversed idler geometry for better filament engagement and reduced eccentricity. Compatible with 8T or 10T motor pinion gears. Drive type: Dual. Used as an upgrade in: Sherpa Mini, custom builds. Ecosystem: Universal.
Verdict Label: Bondtech's precision dual-drive gear assembly — an upgrade kit, not a standalone extruder.
Name: Bondtech RIDGA v2
Pros:
Bondtech precision-machined hardened steel gears
Improved reversed idler geometry vs standard BMG
Compatible with 8T and 10T motor gears
Drop-in upgrade for Sherpa Mini and BMG-style extruders
All-metal construction — no plastic gear components

Cons: Heavy at 310g (adds significant toolhead mass), expensive at $225 USD, motor-dependent rotation distance, overkill for most home builds
Description: CNC-machined aluminum body extruder with monolithic steel fixed-gear drive. No planetary gearbox — the motor drives directly through a fixed reduction. Rotation distance varies by motor: 7.39 (FXD Pro Motor), 5.29 (Moons N14 10T), 4.23 (LDO 8T N14). Premium build quality targeting high-cycle precision printing.
Name: FXD v1.1
Pros: CNC aluminum body for maximum rigidity, monolithic steel gears for durability, no plastic gearbox to crack or wear, premium feel

Cons:
Heavier than Orbiter/Sherpa alternatives — not ideal for mass-optimized CoreXY toolheads
Bulkier body limits compatibility in tight toolhead designs
Higher price than open-source alternatives
LGX Lite V2 now available — this version slightly dated
1.75mm only — no 2.85mm support
Description: Compact version of Bondtech's Large Gears eXtruder (LGX), designed for direct-drive setups. Uses Bondtech's dual-drive large gear technology. Includes a matched 36mm round stepper motor with 10T motor gear. Supports 1.75mm filament only. Brand: Bondtech. Drive type: Dual (large BMG-style gears). Klipper: gear_ratio 44:10. LGX Lite V2 available as incremental update. Ecosystem: Multi — Prusa MK3/4 retrofit, Voron, CoreXY.
Verdict Label: Bondtech build quality in a compact form — reliable dual-drive but heavier than Orbiter/Sherpa alternatives.
Name: LGX Lite
Pros:
Bondtech build quality with hardened dual-drive large gears
Includes matched 36mm round stepper motor
Proven reliability across Prusa and Voron ecosystems
Widely stocked through Bondtech global reseller network
Known-good idler tension system — reliable long-term

Cons: Requires Galileo 2 gear kit purchased separately; less community testing than WristWatch BMG; niche application
Description: Combines the proven 9:1 planetary gearing from the Galileo 2 with the Orbiter 2 mounting footprint. Designed by @bythorsthunder, repository maintained by tetsu97. A bridge between two popular extruder families — useful when your toolhead has an Orbiter mount but you want planetary reduction.
Verdict Label: Niche Planetary — Galileo 2 guts in an Orbiter mount footprint
Name: WristWatch G2
Pros: Galileo 2 planetary internals (9:1 reduction); Orbiter 2 mount pattern; free and open source; compact; bridges two popular extruder families

Cons: Requires BMG gear kit purchased separately; printed body; HevORT-specific mount limits cross-platform compatibility
Description: The original HextrudORT by MirageC79, designed for the HevORT printer's carriage. Uses Bondtech BMG gearing (50:17 dual drive) in an ultra-compact printed body. The Vz-HextrudORT in this database is the VzBot community's adaptation — for HevORT builds, this is the reference design.
Verdict Label: HevORT-Native — BMG gearing in an ultra-light HevORT carriage mount
Name: HextrudORT
Pros: Designed specifically for HevORT carriage; BMG-derived dual drive (50:17); ultra-light printed body; free/OSS; source design for the popular VzBot community adaptation

Cons:
Requires HGX-Lite gear kit — additional cost on top of printed parts
Smaller community install base vs Sherpa Mini or Orbiter
Printed plastic body — less rigid than CNC alternatives
Fewer pre-built toolhead integrations than LGX Lite or Sherpa
Description: Print-it-yourself compact direct drive extruder by nhchiu (also the designer of ProtoXtruder). Uses HGX-Lite large drive gears (44:10, 37:17 ratio) in a compact body with the same mounting footprint as the Bondtech LGX Lite. Features a thickened idler arm vs original design to prevent flex under load. Supports 3 types of 4mm OD PTFE tube retainers. Available on Printables and GitHub (nhchiu/VoronMods). Drive type: Dual (HGX-Lite gears). Ecosystem: Voron / CoreXY.
Verdict Label: Free-to-print LGX Lite-footprint extruder using HGX-Lite gears — strong dual-drive grip, zero cost beyond the gear kit.
Name: Hummingbird
Pros:
LGX Lite mounting footprint — wide toolhead compatibility
HGX-Lite gears provide strong dual-drive grip at high ratio
Thickened idler arm prevents flex under sustained load
Print-it-yourself — zero cost beyond HGX-Lite gear kit
By nhchiu — active Voron community contributor (ProtoXtruder designer)

Cons:
Newer product with smaller community install base
Limited documentation compared to Sherpa Mini
Niche form factor — most builders don't need this slim profile
Description: The Lite Pro Slim Repack is Lettucehead3D's production version of the Lite Pro extruder in a slimmed-down repackaged form factor. Designed for toolhead builds where standard extruder body depth is a constraint.
Verdict Label: A slim, high-ratio compact extruder for space-constrained toolheads — Lettucehead3D's production repack.
Name: Lite Pro Slim Repack
Pros:
Slim profile fits tight toolhead designs
Production quality from Lettucehead3D
High gear ratio for increased extrusion torque
Lightweight design reduces toolhead moving mass

Cons: $150 is expensive vs. community alternatives; heavier than plastic-body LGX Lite; overkill for non-heated-chamber builds
Description: The all-CNC aluminum version of the Bondtech LGX Lite. Eliminates body flex under high acceleration or elevated chamber temperatures. Same gear ratio and LGX Lite mount compatibility makes it a direct upgrade from the standard LGX Lite. The practical choice when printing at sustained high temps where a plastic body would creep or deform.
Verdict Label: Premium LGX Lite — CNC aluminum for heated chamber and high-speed builds
Name: Bondtech LGX Lite PRO
Pros: CNC aluminum body eliminates plastic flex under heat or high acceleration; same gear ratio and LGX Lite mount as the standard LGX Lite; direct drop-in upgrade; Bondtech reliability and support
